title: Lohgarh and the Gurus' coins
hook: Banda strikes coins and seals in the name of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh
tomorrow: Land to those who work it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chappar Chiri: an ending arrived, but couldn't give back what was lost. Your line was it came. Today, something small enough to hold in your palm.

Take a coin out of a pocket or a purse and turn it over. There's usually a name on it, or a face, or a seal: whoever claims the right to say this metal is worth something. A coin says who rules here. So it means something that once Banda Singh held territory, he made his base in the hills at a fort called Lohgarh, and from there he struck coins and stamped seals. The question is whose name went on them.
screen: `TURN A COIN OVER.` → `A NAME SAYS WHO RULES HERE.` → `COINS STRUCK AT LOHGARH.`

segments.voice: Banda Singh now had a fort, an army and lands under his hand. He could have stamped his own name. He didn't. Sikh tradition says the coins and the seal were struck in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, the first Guru and the tenth. Remember the instructions tradition says came with the five arrows: never set yourself up as a Guru, and remember you serve the Khalsa. The coins look like that instruction made into metal. The power was real, but the name on it belonged to someone else. The words on his seal were in Persian, and as Sikh tradition reads them, they speak of deg and tegh. The deg is the cooking pot, the great kettle of the langar where anyone can eat. The tegh is the sword, raised to protect. Pot and sword, side by side, as the gift of the Gurus: a short summary of what the Khalsa was meant to be. Feed people, and defend them. Some readers hear in these coins the stamp of Sikh rule. Others hear something quieter: a man with every chance to make his own name large chose to stamp the names of his Gurus instead. On an ordinary day the pull is the same in small ways: the report with our name at the top, the credit we'd like to keep. The coins of Lohgarh point the other way.
screen: `HE COULD HAVE STAMPED HIS OWN NAME.` ·`BANDA SINGH STAMPED THE GURUS' NAMES.` · `DEG AND TEGH: POT AND SWORD.` · `FEED PEOPLE, AND DEFEND THEM.` · then, large: `IN THEIR NAMES.`

segments.voice: Hold a coin if one is near, or picture one, and read what's on it slowly: whose name, whose face, whose words. Then ask what name you'd want stamped on the things you make, your work, your kindness, your choices; maybe someone who taught you, maybe Waheguru. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out as you hold it.
Deg tegh, the cooking pot and the sword. The gift of the Gurus, stamped into the seal Banda Singh struck at Lohgarh, in his Gurus' names.
Your line: in their names. The pot and the sword, and someone else's name on both. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 841 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LAND TO THOSE WHO WORK IT.`

howItsDone: Sikhs remember that Banda Singh Bahadur struck coins and a seal at Lohgarh in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh rather than his own, and the words deg and tegh are still used for the Khalsa's twin duty to feed and to protect.
